title: Grill — Harness account stacks (round 2: push-back + remaining shape)
summary:
Round 1 settled the stack model, the v1 kinds (Claude + Codex), the limit signals, mid-turn continuation, exact session transfer and the all-exhausted behavior. Four answers went against the evidence and need a second look before they can go into the plan:

- **Copy credential files** — this makes the backup authenticate as the primary account, so it shares the primary's quota and does not provide failover.
- **Mirror everything, including settings and hooks** — hooks execute shell code and `settings.json` `env` can carry API keys.
- **Claude + Codex only** — but the acceptance default you confirmed still mentions an OpenCode adapter.
- **No maximum stack size** — fine for the data, but the UI cannot assume a short list.

There are also **7 remaining shape decisions** (after-swap direction, HOME-override git/ssh, swap notice, orphaned work, lifecycle, manual switches, synthetic prompt) and **5 defaults** at the end.
proven: Round 1 settled: an **implicit chain attached to each account**; **same-kind only**; **Claude Code + Codex** for v1; **preempt Claude's auto-continue** and swap immediately; limits are **quota + 429 + 402/credits** only; mid-turn uses **exact continuation**; history means the **exact provider session**; all-exhausted is **auto-retry at the earliest reset, cap 3**; name is **harness stack**; no maximum size; the task stays running with a suppressed failure toast; the swap intent is persisted and boot-reconciled.

The acceptance answer carries a note: tests do **not** need a real Claude account. The repo already has fake drivers (`AGETOR_CLAUDE_DRIVER=fake`, `AGETOR_CODEX_DRIVER=fake`) and `AGETOR_FAKE_CLAUDE_API_ERROR`; the plan will use those, not live credentials.

sections.title: Push-back on round-1 overrides
sections.intro: These are the answers that conflict with the investigation or with each other. Each one changes the plan's security or scope, so I would rather re-ask than silently build it.

questions.title: Copying the primary's credential files makes the backup the same provider account. Do you still want that?
questions.why: A provider token identifies an account, not a machine. If the backup uses the primary's token, it consumes the primary's quota and hits the same limit, so the train has no extra capacity. The token also lands in an agent-writable home, and copying it may violate provider terms.
questions.context: In round 1 you chose **Copy credential files between homes** over each member using its own login. The investigation's security assumption is the opposite: never copy `.credentials.json`, `auth.json`, `cli-config.json`, OpenCode's credential tables or any token blob. The practical contradiction: a backup account is supposed to be a *different account* with its own quota. If it authenticates with the primary's token, the provider sees one account and the 5-hour/weekly limit is shared. That is useful for a second CLI install of the same login, but it is not failover.

evidence.label: the investigation's credential boundary
evidence.code: 2. **Each member is already logged in and configured for itself.** Agetor must never copy `.credentials.json`, `auth.json`, `cli-config.json`, the OpenCode account/credential tables or any token blob between accounts. If a member is logged out, it is skipped (or the swap fails with a clear message), not repaired by copying another account's auth.

evidence.label: only the master token is scrubbed today
alias credentials are a plain file in an agent-writable home

options.label: Each member uses its own login
options.description: Revert to the recommendation: never copy tokens; a logged-out member is skipped with a clear message and the existing harness login flow sets it up.
options.consequence: The backup is a genuinely different account with its own quota. This is the only option that makes the train add capacity.

options.label: Keep copying, but accept it is the same account
options.description: Copy the primary's credential files into the backup's home. The backup authenticates as the primary, shares its quota, and is useful only as a second CLI installation of the same login.
options.consequence: Needs a security review, an explicit warning in the UI, and a name that does not promise failover. The train cannot survive the primary's limit because the backup is the primary.

options.label: Let the user paste the backup's own token
options.description: The backup's token is obtained from that account separately and stored in its own home; Agetor never reads the primary's credential file.
options.consequence: Still a token in an agent-writable home, but it is a different account and the quota is separate. More manual setup than the existing login flow.

options.label: Share a keychain item by reference
options.description: Point the backup at the primary's keychain item.
options.consequence: Same-account quota problem, and only works for the built-in Claude account; not portable to alias homes or Codex.

recommendation.reason: A backup that uses the primary's token is the same account to the provider, so it cannot provide the extra quota the feature exists for; the token-in-an-agent-writable-home problem is a second reason.

questions.title: "Mirror everything" includes hooks and permissions, which execute code. What exactly should be mirrored?
questions.why: Hooks run arbitrary shell commands on every tool call; permissions change what the agent may do without asking; `settings.json` `env` can carry API keys. Mirroring them into another account's home is a security boundary, not a convenience setting.
questions.context: In round 1 you chose **Mirror everything, including settings and hooks** over copying the safe subset. That is a bigger change than it sounds: Claude's `settings.json` can contain `hooks`, `permissions`, `env` and `mcpServers`; Codex's `config.toml` can contain model/provider settings and MCP servers. A mirror that copies `env` could copy a key; a mirror that copies hooks makes the backup execute the primary's code. The investigation's safe-subset option excluded credentials, OAuth tokens, hooks and permissions.

evidence.label: what Agetor already discovers per kind
the safe-subset recommendation
evidence.code: - **Inject per kind (larger v1):** Claude `--mcp-config` (merged JSON) + a generated/copied skills/plugin dir; cursor/fx ACP `mcpServers` + skill dir copy; OpenCode share the config dir only (not the data/auth dir); codex config merge; copilot `mcp-config.json`/skills copy; gemini/antigravity selective settings/skills. All must exclude credential files.

options.label: Mirror the safe subset only
options.description: MCP server definitions, skills, commands and plugins; non-executable settings. Exclude hooks, permission rules, `env`, credentials and OAuth tokens.
options.consequence: The backup can use the same tools and skills without inheriting code that runs on every tool call. A backup-local hook/permission set stays the user's choice.
options.preview:
MIRROR:  mcpServers, skills/, commands/, plugins/installed_plugins.json
KEEP LOCAL: hooks, permissions, env, .credentials.json, auth.json

options.label: Include hooks and permissions, exclude credentials
options.description: Mirror the full `settings.json`/`config.toml` except credential and token fields.
options.consequence: The backup behaves exactly like the primary, including its hooks and permission posture. Needs a security review, a visible warning, and a per-kind allowlist that strips `env`/token fields.

options.label: Mirror the whole file, including `env`
options.description: Copy `settings.json`/`config.toml` as-is, excluding only the known credential files.
options.consequence: Highest fidelity and highest risk: an `env` block can carry an API key into another account's home. Needs a credential scan and a security review.

options.label: Safe subset, but only on a manual Sync
options.description: Same allowlist as the safe subset, but nothing is copied until the user presses "Sync from primary" in Settings.
options.consequence: Most predictable; the user sees exactly when a config moved. A new MCP server does not reach the backup until the user syncs.

recommendation.reason: It delivers the tools and skills the backup needs without copying code that executes on every tool call or an `env` block that can carry a key.

questions.title: You chose Claude + Codex only, but the acceptance default you confirmed mentions an OpenCode adapter. Which is the v1 scope?
questions.why: The plan's task list, adapter work and test matrix depend on the exact kind set. An acceptance criterion that names a kind outside the scope will fail the build or silently drop a promised test.
questions.context: In round 1 you answered **Claude Code and Codex for now** (overriding the recommended Claude + Codex + OpenCode). Separately, you accepted the acceptance default that says **per-kind adapter tests for Codex and OpenCode**. OpenCode's transfer is proven (S3), but it is the only one of the three that is a *move* rather than a copy, so its adapter is the most expensive. Pick the scope that the plan and the acceptance bar will both use.

evidence.label: S3: OpenCode transfer is proven but is a move

options.label: Claude + Codex only
options.description: Keep your round-1 scope. Drop the OpenCode adapter from v1; the acceptance bar becomes a Claude e2e plus a Codex adapter test.
options.consequence: Smallest v1 and the fastest path. OpenCode users see "stacks are not supported for this kind yet".

options.label: Add OpenCode back
options.description: Use the original recommendation: Claude + Codex + OpenCode, with the acceptance bar as written.
options.consequence: One more adapter and its move-not-merge edge cases; the acceptance bar needs no change.

options.label: Claude only
options.description: Narrow further to the best-supported kind.
options.consequence: Fastest, but Codex users are excluded even though their transfer is proven.

recommendation.reason: It respects your explicit scope answer; the acceptance bar should be edited to match rather than quietly keeping a test for a kind that is not in v1.

sections.title: Remaining shape decisions
sections.intro: These are the lifecycle and UX decisions round 1 did not cover. They change the plan's task list but not the core model.

questions.title: After a swap, where does the task run next?
questions.why: "Train" can mean forward-only, wrap-around, or return-to-primary. It decides whether the plan needs reset timers on the task and how much churn a long task sees.
questions.context: A stack is ordered. The simplest model: a task moves forward when the current member limits, and a new task starts at the head (skipping cooling members). A reset-aware return adds timers and can bounce a long task between accounts, transferring the session each time. The all-exhausted answer already adds a reset timer for the end of the train.

options.label: Forward only within a task
options.description: Stay on the current member until it limits, then move forward. A new task starts at the head, skipping cooling members.
options.consequence: Predictable, no mid-task bounce. The primary is retried naturally on the next task, not in the middle of the current one.

options.label: Wrap to the first reset member
options.description: After the last member, wrap to the first one whose quota has reset.
options.consequence: Keeps a very long task running, but can bounce between accounts and repeat session transfers.

options.label: Return to the primary when it resets
options.description: As soon as the primary's quota resets, move the task back to it, even mid-task.
options.consequence: Most "primary-first", but the most churn and the most timers. A task could transfer twice in one turn.

recommendation.reason: A new task already retries the primary; bouncing a live task mid-turn adds transfers and side-effect risk for no quota benefit.

questions.title: Codex aliases override HOME, so the backup loses `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.config/gh` and `~/.npmrc`. What should v1 do?
questions.why: Codex is in your v1 set. A swap from the built-in Codex account to an alias can turn a working commit or push into a failure without any provider limit. This is the most visible "seamless" gap for the chosen kinds.
questions.context: `harnessEnv` sets `HOME=<home>` for Codex (and cursor/fx/antigravity/opencode). Claude, Gemini and Copilot keep the real HOME and only redirect their own config var. A HOME overlay would symlink or copy the standard dotfiles while keeping the CLI's own state dirs separate; the investigation calls it a separate, broad feature. Restricting stacks to accounts with the same HOME profile would prevent the main built-in + alias Codex case.

evidence.label: codex re-homes the whole process
the investigation's options
evidence.code:
21. **For kinds that override `HOME` (codex, cursor, fx, antigravity, opencode), must the backup keep the user's git/ssh/gh/npm config?**
    Why: a full `HOME` override hides `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.config/gh`, etc. A stack moving from the built-in to such an account can no longer commit/sign/push the same way. Options: HOME overlay, restrict stacks to accounts with the same HOME profile, or document the limitation.

options.label: Document it and warn at stack creation
options.description: No overlay in v1. The stack editor and the first swap show a clear warning that a HOME-override account does not see the main home's git/ssh/gh/npm config.
options.consequence: Smallest scope; the limitation is honest. A Codex backup can still edit files but may fail to commit, sign or push.

options.label: Build a HOME overlay for the five kinds
options.description: Give each alias home a shared overlay that symlinks the standard dotfiles (`~/.gitconfig`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.config/gh`, `~/.npmrc`) while keeping the CLI's own state dirs separate.
options.consequence: Closest to seamless and the best fit for Codex, but it is a broad, security-sensitive feature: symlinks into `.ssh` and `.config/gh`, per-account setup, and tests for every HOME-override kind.

options.label: Only stack accounts with the same HOME profile
options.description: A built-in Codex account cannot be stacked with a HOME-override alias.
options.consequence: No broken git/ssh, but it blocks the main built-in + backup Codex case, which is the reason to build the feature.

recommendation.reason: The overlay is a separate, broad feature; v1 should not silently promise it. The warning is cheap and keeps the limitation visible at the moment the stack is created.

questions.title: What should the in-transcript swap message look like?
questions.why: The notice is the user's only proof the swap happened. The existing `status` stream is persisted and already rendered by the RunPanel, the CLI and the TUI; a dedicated card needs a new event shape and three renderers.
questions.context: RunPanel renders `status` events as a muted `StatusDivider`; `isInternalStatusSentinel` suppresses internal sentinel lines, so a visible swap line must not use one of those prefixes. The status stream is also what `agetor logs` and the TUI render. A structured payload (from/to/reason/position/reset) can still be a divider and give all three surfaces the data for free.

evidence.label: the existing divider
status is the persisted transcript channel
internal sentinels are suppressed

options.label: A status divider with structured text
options.description: e.g. `Switched to Codex — Work · limit reached · 2/3`. Persisted on the `status` stream; rendered by the RunPanel, CLI and TUI.
options.consequence: Cheapest and consistent with existing status lines. No new event type; the CLI/TUI get it for free.

options.label: A dedicated card
options.description: A richer block with from/to, reason, reset time and actions (switch back, pin to this account).
options.consequence: Nicer in the RunPanel, but a new event shape and three renderers; the CLI/TUI need a fallback.

options.label: Divider in the transcript, card in the run panel
options.description: The divider is the durable record; the card is the interactive surface.
options.consequence: Most complete, but both implementations and a rule for when each appears.

recommendation.reason: The user asked for a message in the middle of the task messages; the status stream already gives that on every surface, and a structured payload leaves room for a card later.

questions.title: What happens to pending permission/question cards, running background agents, and queued follow-ups when the account swaps?
questions.why: They belong to the old session and cannot move with the transcript. Dropping a user's typed follow-up loses work; carrying a permission card to a different process is impossible; waiting for a background agent can delay the failover forever.
questions.context: `dropSession` orphans subagents; `reconcileTaskSession` currently drops every queued follow-up on a harness change but does not call `cancelPendingForTask`. The swap path must be more careful than the manual switch: cancel the old session's cards, keep the user's typed follow-ups, and name any abandoned background agents in a status line.

evidence.label: the existing drain order
evidence.code: async function drainFollowUpQueues(taskId: string, runId: string, wasCancelled: boolean): Promise<void> {

evidence.label: a manual harness change drops the queue today

options.label: Cancel cards, keep follow-ups, name abandoned agents
options.description: Cancel pending permission/question cards on the old account; keep the user's queued follow-ups and drain them after the new run settles; abandon background agents with a status line naming them.
options.consequence: The user's typed text is not lost, and the swap is not blocked by a subagent that may never finish. The abandoned agent's work is visible, not silent.

options.label: Move follow-ups to the backlog tray
options.description: Cancel cards and put queued follow-ups back in the task's backlog so the user decides when to send them.
options.consequence: Safest for intent, but the user has to re-send; the task does not continue seamlessly.

options.label: Cancel cards and drop the queue
options.description: The current manual-switch behavior.
options.consequence: Simple, but loses the user's typed text at the worst moment.

options.label: Wait for background agents first
options.description: Delay the swap until running subagents finish (or a timeout).
options.consequence: Avoids abandoning work, but the failover can be delayed indefinitely and the old account is already limited.

recommendation.reason: It preserves the user's text and the task's momentum while being honest about the background work that cannot move.

questions.title: When a stack is created or a member is disabled, deleted, reordered or removed, when do tasks pick up the change?
questions.why: Under the implicit model a stack is a property of the account, so adding a backup silently changes every existing task on that account. This decides whether that is immediate, next-turn, or only for new tasks.
questions.context: A running turn is on a live process; a new turn resolves `Task.agent` again. Disabling a harness skips it for new runs but leaves in-flight runs alone. Deleting a harness is already refused if any task or profile references the row (`harnesses.delete`). Removing a member that no task currently uses is safe; removing the active member of a running task is not.

evidence.label: delete refuses while tasks/profiles reference the row
a disabled harness refuses new runs only
evidence.code:
/** Soft-delete flag. Disabled harnesses are hidden from the New Task
   *  picker, the default-harness selector, and the window topbar, but the
   *  row stays in the DB so historical `tasks.agent = <id>` references
   *  keep resolving. The orchestrator refuses to start new runs on a
   *  disabled harness; in-flight runs are unaffected.

options.label: At the next turn
options.description: Existing tasks use the new stack/membership at their next turn; the in-flight turn finishes on the current account. Disabling skips the member; removing it from the stack applies to the next selection; deleting it removes the membership (the existing delete check still protects a row a task is on).
options.consequence: No killed turns and no surprise mid-turn moves. A task already running on a member that was just disabled finishes its current turn, then moves on.

options.label: Only tasks created after the change
options.description: Existing tasks keep a snapshot of the stack as it was when they were created.
options.consequence: Predictable for existing work, but needs a per-task snapshot and makes the account's stack membership inconsistent across tasks.

options.label: Repoint in-flight tasks immediately
options.description: Kill the current turn and move it to the next member.
options.consequence: Not seamless; can duplicate or lose work. Only makes sense for a manual "switch now" action.

options.label: Refuse membership changes while tasks reference the member
options.description: Deleting/disabling/reordering a member is blocked until every task on it is idle or moved.
options.consequence: Safest for live work, but makes stack cleanup painful and blocks a user who just wants to remove a backup.

recommendation.reason: It matches the existing disabled-harness semantics and never kills a live turn; the delete check already protects a row a task is actually on.

questions.title: When the user manually switches a task to another member of the same stack, should the conversation be preserved?
questions.why: Today any harness-id change kills the session and drops queued follow-ups. If a manual switch inside a stack behaves differently from an automatic swap, the stack's promise becomes inconsistent.
questions.context: `reconcileTaskSession` treats any harness-id change as a session-killing event, including a same-kind alias swap, and drops every queued follow-up. A manual switch inside the stack could use the same transfer path as an automatic swap; a switch outside the stack should keep today's reset behavior.

evidence.label: any harness change kills the session

options.label: Preserve within the stack, reset outside
options.description: A manual switch to a member of the same stack uses the transfer path and keeps the queue; a switch to an account outside the stack keeps today's reset behavior.
options.consequence: Consistent with automatic swaps and with the stack's promise. Needs the manual path to distinguish "same stack" from "different account".

options.label: Keep today's reset behavior
options.description: Only automatic swaps preserve the conversation; any manual switch starts fresh.
options.consequence: Simpler and matches the current rule, but a user who manually picks the backup loses the context the stack just promised.

recommendation.reason: A manual switch between members of the same stack is the same move as an automatic swap; making it reset would be the surprising behavior.

questions.title: Should the synthetic "continue" prompt be visible in the transcript?
questions.why: Agetor's rule is that it never adds its own text to a user message. A continuation prompt is a new exception, and a later JSONL rebuild must be able to tell it apart from a real user message.
questions.context: The only machine-added text today is the references heading, the agent-instructions wrapper, the issue warning, the pipeline step prompt and the handoff reminder. A hidden prompt needs a tag (e.g. `harness_swap`) in `user-message.ts` or a run-level synthetic flag. The swap notice is the visible record either way.

evidence.label: the no-added-text rule
evidence.code: - **Agetor never adds its own text to a message, and nothing it puts in a prompt names the product**, for any harness. The only machine-added text around a prompt is the references block heading, the `<agent_instructions_defined_by_the_user>` wrapper, the issue-thread untrusted-content warning, and the pipeline step prompt and handoff reminder.

options.label: Hidden from the transcript, tagged in storage
options.description: The continuation prompt is stored as a synthetic user message with a `harness_swap` tag; the visible record is the swap notice.
options.consequence: Clean transcript, and a rebuild can distinguish it. Needs the tag in the shared user-message parser and a renderer rule.

options.label: Visible as a system block
options.description: Render a small system block: "Agetor asked the backup to continue from the transferred session."
options.consequence: Transparent, but adds noise to every swap and needs a new renderer in the RunPanel/CLI/TUI.

options.label: No synthetic prompt
options.description: Resume the session without any added text.
options.consequence: Some providers will not continue a turn without a user message; the backup may sit idle or repeat the last turn.

recommendation.reason: The swap notice is the user-facing record; the continuation prompt is machinery, and tagging it keeps the no-added-text rule honest.

sections.title: Confirm or override
sections.intro: Defaults that follow from round 1. One click each, or override with what it should be.

questions.title: How is the next member chosen?

recommendation.value: Both: skip a member whose cached quota clearly says exhausted, and react to a failure as the backstop. A stale or missing snapshot never blocks a run on its own.
recommendation.reason: Only three kinds have quota and the poll is 10 minutes old; proactive is an optimization, reactive is the guarantee.

questions.title: Is exhaustion account-global or per task?

recommendation.value: Account-global: a new `harness_limit_state` table (no FK, like `harness_usage`) with `exhausted_until_ms`, reason, source and message. Selection skips a cooling account in every task; it clears on a successful turn or on expiry. No concurrency reservation in v1.
recommendation.reason: Quota is account-global; a per-task cooldown would make N tasks each discover the same limit and swap to the same backup.

questions.title: What follows from "no maximum" stack size?

recommendation.value: No hard cap. The stack editor virtualizes long lists and shows a warning above 10 members; the swap UI shows position/count; selection stays O(n) per turn.
recommendation.reason: No maximum is fine for the data, but the picker, the editor and the topbar must not assume a short list.

recommendation.value: No global feature flag. Stacks are opt-in by creating one, so an existing user sees no behavior change until they build a stack.
recommendation.reason: The feature is inert without a stack; a flag would add a second code path for no safety benefit.

questions.title: Can a single task opt out of failover?

recommendation.value: No per-task opt-out in v1. A task that must stay on one account uses an account that is not in a stack.
recommendation.reason: The implicit model makes the stack a property of the account; a per-task flag adds a column and a UI control for a rare case.
